title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache cost model (OceanPay)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked OceanPay through Redwood Optimize focusing on batching and KV/prefix caching strategies and a cost model. Covered traffic shapes, latency SLOs, batch vs latency tradeoffs, cache warmup, and pilot plan. Customer requested security/KMS details and a benchmark pilot. Agreed next steps: share cost model, run bench, schedule pilot kickoff after infra whitelisting.
topics: Prefix vs KV cache behavior and TTLs
Cost model spreadsheet and token math

transcript:
Header: 2027-09-30 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Jamie Park, Ravi Patel, Ana Gomez (Redwood); Maya Chen, Luis Ortega, Priya Rao, Ethan Lopez (OceanPay)

[00:00] Jamie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for making time - this is Jamie from Redwood, AE - we also have Ravi (SE) and Ana on the call.
[00:04] Maya Chen: Hi yeah thanks, we wanted a deep dive on optimize - specifically batching and that k v cache thing you mentioned in the deck.
[00:10] Ravi Patel: Cool, we'll start with a quick recap of your goals then jump into the cost model and a live sim of cache behavior. Sorry in advance if audio glitches - my mic is meh today.
[00:18] Luis Ortega: No worries, we have limited time - our core ask: keep P99 latency < 200ms for customer-facing flows, and cut per-token inference cost by ~30% from current self-hosted infra.
[00:27] Jamie Park: Great, that's helpful. Maya, can you confirm traffic shape? Percent of short vs long sequences?
[00:33] Maya Chen: We see 65% under 64 tokens, 25% between 64-256, and about 10% long tails >512 but those are low qps.
[00:40] Ravi Patel: Perfect. That distribution is very amenable to prefix/KV caching. Quick note: "prefix cache" here means reusing KV for repeated prefixes across sessions; KV cache is per-conversation K V store - apologies if terms get sloshed.
[00:52] Ana Gomez: I'll drop the terminology slide in the follow-up deck; sometimes transcriptions show K V as separate letters - it's kv-cache.
[01:00] Jamie Park: Alright jump to slide 4 (we shared the deck link in the calendar): batching overview. The key tradeoff is batch size vs latency. Larger batch => better GPU utilization => lower cost per token but higher queuing latency.
[01:14] Priya Rao: How deterministic is queuing? Our user flows are bursty - peak qps during auth flows.
[01:20] Ravi Patel: We recommend dynamic batching with latency SLOs: target a micro-batch window (10-30ms) for low-latency tiers. For your P99 200ms goal, we propose micro-batch window 15ms plus a fast-path dedicated fleet for <10ms tail.
[01:36] Ethan Lopez: Dedicated fleet meaning reserved GPU pool? We have security constraints so dedicated sounds better anyway.
[01:41] Jamie Park: Yes Dedicated pools (Redwood Dedicated) or private deployment. For the pilot we can run in our hosted environment but with isolated capacity or we can help set up a VPC-hosted dedicated pool - tradeoffs: hosted quicker, dedicated gives isolation and easier SSO/KMS integration.
[01:58] Luis Ortega: About KV cache: initial warmup costs worry us - if cache cold, we'd pay cost for full sequences then later cheaper? How is that accounted in the cost model?
[02:07] Ravi Patel: Good question. In our cost model we simulate cold-start token spend and amortize over expected hit rates. Essentially two levers - hit-rate and TTL. If you have many repeated prefixes (customer prompts, templates), hit-rate can be high and amortized cost drops significantly.
[02:22] Jamie Park: We'll show the spreadsheet in a sec - it models tokens billed (input+generated) and then subtracts tokens avoided by KV hits.
[02:30] Maya Chen: Could you walk through a concrete example? Say 70% short seqs under 64, and 20% reuse of prefixes from templates.
[02:37] Ravi Patel: Sure. Example: baseline per-token cost $0.00006. With batching/quantization + caching we model a 28-38% reduction in unit cost depending on hit-rate and batch distribution. So for your mix (70% short, 20% prefix reuse) the spreadsheet shows ~32% saving at steady state. Cold start week shows less, but after warmup it reaches that band.
[02:56] [03:00] Jamie Park: (unintelligible) the sim link is in chat - https://redwood.ai/spreadsheets/cost-model-oceanpay - note it's view-only.
[03:08] Priya Rao: Saw it, thanks. There's a tab called "pilot config" - what's the recommended TTL on prefix cache?
[03:14] Ravi Patel: Good callout - TTL depends on how dynamic the prompts are. For templates and system prompts we usually set TTL long (hours-days). For user-specific conversational KV we set short (minutes) to limit staleness and memory. In the spreadsheet we model TTL as cache eviction window which impacts hit-rate.
[03:30] Luis Ortega: Security: can cached KVs contain PII? We need to ensure it doesn't persist beyond retention policy and integrates with our KMS.
[03:37] Ana Gomez: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS and configurable TTL + auto-purge. For Private deployments you can enforce no-persist mode where KV lives only in-VM and is wiped after response. We'll attach the security notes.
[03:50] Maya Chen: How does batching interact with streaming responses? Some UX requires token-by-token streaming for typing indicators.
[03:56] Ravi Patel: We support streaming with batch-aware emit - fast-path streaming uses micro-batches and immediately flushes partial outputs. There's a slight throughput penalty if you force token-level streaming for every request, but we can tier routes: streaming route with smaller batch, non-streaming with larger batch.
[04:14] Jamie Park: Let's demo the KV-hit sim - Ravi, take it away.
[04:18] [04:18] Ravi Patel: I'm going to share my screen now - apologies if draw is laggy. (sound of mouse) Alright here's a simple sim: inputs, hit-rate slider, TTL slider, batch window slider. You can see cost per 1M tokens updates as we change hit-rate.
[04:33] Ravi Patel: At 0% hit-rate cost is baseline. At 40% hit-rate cost drops by ~24% with our recommended batch windows; at 60% it drops near 36%. Notice how TTL also interacts because higher TTL increases hit-rate for repeat templates but raises memory usage.
[04:52] Ethan Lopez: For memory - what are the resource impacts on GPU memory vs CPU? Is KV kept on host memory?
[05:00] Ravi Patel: The KV cache is managed in host RAM and optionally in GPU memory for ultra-low-latency hot keys. By default it's host RAM; we can configure a hot cache on device if you want sub-10ms tails but that moves memory cost to GPU. We'll capture that in the cost model as an optional premium.
[05:18] Priya Rao: Can Redwood auto-tune batch windows based on observed latency?
[05:22] Ana Gomez: Yes, Optimize has an auto-suggest feature - it proposes micro-batch windows and batch sizes given observed latency/throughput, and includes simulation for rollback to faster config if SLOs slip. We'll show recommended profiles in the pilot tab.
[05:36] [06:00] Luis Ortega: Ok let's talk pilot - what's realistic scope and timeline?
[06:05] Jamie Park: We recommend a 4-week pilot: week 0-1 setup and whitelisting, week 2 run benchmarks (2-4h runs covering normal + peak traffic), week 3-4 evaluate cost/run tuning and signoff. Success criteria: P99 <200ms on targeted routes and >=25% reduction in per-token inference spend vs baseline.
[06:25] Maya Chen: Are there any hidden costs in instrumentation / egress? We worry about cost outside token billing.
[06:31] Ravi Patel: Good call - the cost model includes compute tokens and optional device premium; networking/egress is separate. We'll show a row for egress in the spreadsheet but that is usually minor for API calls unless you stream huge assets.
[06:44] Jamie Park: Also noted security review timeline - if you want Redwood Private we need to start legal + infra conversations now. We'll drop the security packet.
[06:52] Priya Rao: On SLAs and rollback - if a rollout increases errors what automatic fallback exists?
[06:58] Ana Gomez: Redwood supports route-level fallback to a lower-cost or higher-compatibility model and automated canary checks with health gates. If error rate spikes, traffic auto-shifts to fallback and we notify.
[07:12] [07:20] Maya Chen: Quick question from Ethan: how do you bill cache savings? Do we see negative tokens?
[07:25] Ravi Patel: We don't bill negative tokens. Billing is still based on tokens processed by runtime; when KV cache avoids recomputing tokens we simply see fewer billed tokens. Our billing export will show the reduced tokens and we provide a reconciliation spreadsheet.
[07:36] Luis Ortega: Any compliance concerns for storing cache across regions? We need EU-only for some datasets.
[07:42] Ana Gomez: You can pin cache region to data residency; for Private you'd control the region fully. Hosted we can provision region-isolated pools.
[07:50] Jamie Park: Ok wrapping toward the demo part, Ravi will run a benchmark sim for your traffic shape - I might ask you to upload a small synthetic trace after the call.
[07:59] [08:10] Ravi Patel: Running sim now - see the chart: hit-rate ramp vs time, cost per 1k tokens, and latency percentiles. There's a blue line for P50, orange for P95 and red for P99.
[08:22] Ravi Patel: You can see that during warmup P99 spikes due to cold KV - but once templates are populated P99 drops and the cost curve improves. That suggests a warmup strategy: pre-warm prefix cache for known templates during deployment or use short cold-window.
[08:37] Priya Rao: What's the recommended pre-warm approach?
[08:40] Ravi Patel: Either run a short synthetic job to prime caches with recent templates, or route a small percentage of traffic through a warmup job before full cutover. We'll include sample scripts in the repo.
[08:52] Maya Chen: Are those scripts open or do we need access?
[08:55] Ana Gomez: We'll share them in the follow-up GH gist + internal runbook. Link will be in the deck.
[09:02] [09:15] Luis Ortega: I'd like to talk SLA numbers with the account team - what's standard for Dedicated?
[09:19] Jamie Park: For Dedicated we have an SLA offering with uptime and latency targets; specifics get added to the contract. We'll loop in your account exec when we move to DPA.
[09:28] Priya Rao: Two last bits: migration effort for our current inference stack and how Redwood handles model upgrades/rollouts.
[09:35] Ravi Patel: Model upgrades are configurable by version and you can do canary or shadow traffic. We provide a rollout UI and automatic regression detection against your eval prompts. Migration: we support a staged cutover; we can also run endpoints in parallel to compare outputs side-by-side.
[09:49] Jamie Park: Ok let's do recaps and action items. We'll send the cost model spreadsheet and deck, Ravi will prepare benchmark script, Maya will send traffic histogram. We'll aim to kick pilot first week of October pending whitelisting.
[09:59] Maya Chen: Sounds good, thanks everyone. Quick note: a couple of our questions we may ask legal about retention - we'll loop SRE if needed.
[10:06] Jamie Park: Perfect. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the attachments. Thanks all.

Notes: minor transcription errors present (k v vs kv-cache, some speaker overlap). Shared artifacts: deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/oceanpay-optimize  | cost model: https://redwood.ai/spreadsheets/cost-model-oceanpay | pilot scripts gist (to be shared).
